paper_metadata.title: Quantum optimisation via maximally amplified states

summary: The paper introduces the Maximum Amplification Optimisation Algorithm (MAOA), a Grover-style threshold search algorithm that avoids variational optimization and achieves a theoretical speedup of approximately (2r+1) over classical random sampling for combinatorial optimization. Simulations on a 10‑location vehicle routing problem (N ≈ 5.9×10^7) and a 20‑asset portfolio optimization problem (N ≈ 6.2×10^7) show MAOA outperforming restricted Grover adaptive search (RGAS) at rotation counts up to r=128 and r=512 respectively.

experiments.description: Maximum Amplification Optimisation Algorithm (MAOA) applied to a capacitated vehicle routing problem, compared against Grover adaptive search (GAS), restricted Grover adaptive search (RGAS), and classical random sampling.

algorithm.variant: MAOA / truncated Grover-style amplitude amplification with binary thresholding on a complete graph
algorithm.optimizer: Deterministic threshold navigation and adaptive search; no classical variational optimizer used
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Threshold-finding stage: 20 consecutive successful marked measurements at a threshold, otherwise continue scanning; final adaptive search: stop after 40 consecutive successful marked measurements
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial threshold estimated from 200 randomly sampled solutions; threshold search starts near median and steps downward; GAS uses randomized rotation counts from a uniform distribution with growing upper bound

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Solutions correspond to routes over 10 locations; quantum walk/marked-state formulation over the full solution space, with binary marking of solutions below a cost threshold
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Feasibility encoded in the solution space; binary threshold marks solutions with cost below threshold

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Randomly generated instance; integer costs used to increase degeneracy in the quality distribution
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 10,000 simulations for each algorithm/configuration; success probability measured as probability of finding one of the 12 lowest-cost solutions versus computational effort

implementation_details.classical_solver: Nelder-Mead for threshold optimization; classical random sampling baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Precompute solution-quality distribution for the CVRP instance
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Select best solution among measured marked solutions; compute success probability vs effort

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: success probability vs computational effort curves

results.unit: lowest-cost solutions counted as optimal set size
x at r=8; 2r+1 linear scaling claimed

speedup_claims.factor: linear in rotation count; asymptotic speedup 2r+1 over classical random sampling
speedup_claims.conditions: small target-ratio limit; maximally amplified state; restricted circuit depth r
speedup_claims.caveats: Derived from Eq. (18); ignores quantum-walk overhead beyond objective-function calls.

speedup_claims.factor: MAOA outperforms RGAS and both outperform classical random sampling
speedup_claims.caveats: No exact numerical success-probability values are stated in text; comparison is shown in Fig. 9.

speedup_claims.conditions: binary marking on complete graph in low-convergence regime

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(r) per state preparation/measurement; maximum-amplification speedup over classical random sampling scales as O(2r+1) in the small-target-ratio limit
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(e) random sampling; exhaustive search is discussed as a baseline but not the main classical comparator
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: 2r+1 computational effort per prepared/measured amplified state

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not quantified; speedup derived relative to classical random sampling but not against best classical routing algorithms.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires repeated Grover‑style rotations r (tested up to r=128) and ability to prepare a complete‑graph mixing operator over the entire solution space.
limiting_factors: Only compared against classical random sampling rather than state‑of‑the‑art vehicle routing solvers
Speedup depends on oracle evaluation of the cost function inside quantum circuits
Requires large coherent circuits implementing Grover‑style rotations

notes: No physical QPU or simulator platform is named; treated as simulation-based gate-free numerical study, so hardware.type inferred as simulator_other.
The paper reports rotation counts rather than qubit counts; num_qubits is not explicitly stated and remains null.

experiments.description: MAOA applied to a portfolio optimization problem with a low-risk filter and return maximization, compared against GAS, RGAS, and classical random sampling.

algorithm.variant: MAOA / truncated Grover-style amplitude amplification with binary thresholding on a complete graph
algorithm.optimizer: Deterministic threshold navigation and adaptive search; no classical variational optimizer used
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Threshold-finding stage: 20 consecutive successful marked measurements at a threshold, otherwise continue scanning; final adaptive search: stop after 40 consecutive successful marked measurements
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial threshold estimated from 200 randomly sampled solutions; threshold search starts near median and steps downward; GAS uses randomized rotation counts from a uniform distribution with growing upper bound

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Portfolio choices encoded as ternary variables z_i ∈ {-1,0,1} with net position constraint; quantum search is performed over the feasible portfolio space after applying a low-risk threshold and then a return threshold
problem_formulation.objective_function: Maximize expected return subject to a low-risk constraint; return = Σ_i R_i z_i, risk = Σ_{i,j} σ_ij z_i z_j
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Two-threshold marking: first fix risk threshold to lowest 10% of solutions, then mark solutions with return above a threshold within that subspace

problem_instance.description: Portfolio optimization over 20 ASX stocks with net position constraint I=7
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Daily adjusted close prices analyzed to compute expected returns and covariance matrix; risk scaled down by factor 100 in figure
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 10,000 simulations for each algorithm/configuration; success probability measured as probability of finding the single highest-return portfolio among the lowest 10% risk solutions versus computational effort

implementation_details.classical_solver: Nelder-Mead for threshold optimization; classical random sampling baseline
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Compute return/risk distribution from historical market data; fix risk threshold to lowest 10% of solutions
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Select best-return solution among measured marked solutions; compute success probability vs effort

experiments.description: Simulation of MAOA and restricted Grover adaptive search (RGAS) on arbitrarily large optimization problems modeled with a continuous standard normal distribution of solution qualities.

algorithm.variant: MAOA truncated Grover-style amplitude amplification with binary thresholding

key_results: Simulations show MAOA consistently outperforming RGAS when searching for extremely small target ratios (highest‑quality solutions).
Performance curves in Fig. 12 match the theoretical success‑probability model PQ(e, μ, r) = 1 − (1 − μ(2r + 1)^2)^(e/(2r + 1)).
For r = 64, MAOA repeatedly samples from a marked set with approximate ratio ρ ≈ 1/(40(2r + 1)^2) ≈ 1.5 × 10^-6.
